full_judgment:
This rule at the instance of the defendant is directed against the orders dated 10-9-73 and 25-7-74 of the learned Munsif.

2. The plaintiffs filed S.C.C. Suit No. 11 of 1972 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Sylhet exercising jurisdiction of the judge under the S.C.C. Act for evicting the defendant from the premises described in the schedule to the plaint by removing the structures and for recovery of khas possession, on the allegations, inter alia, that the defendant was a defaulter and that he constructed a pucca building without the consent of the plaintiffs who bonafide require the premises.

3. The defendant contested the suit contending , inter alia, that he is a tenant in the said premises for the last 26/27 years at a monthly rental of Tk. 10/-. During the war of liberation, the original structure on the suit premises was burnt into ashes. Thereafter with permission of plaintiff No. 5 he reconstructed a new building incurring a cost of Tk. 50,000/- with full knowledge of the plaintiffs. The defendant, however, dented that he was a defaulter.

4. While the suit was thus proceeding, an application was filed by the plaintiffs for transferring the S.C.C. Suit No. 11 of 1972 into a Title Suit on the statements:

"(1) That the puffs, have filed the aforesaid suit for eviction of the defdt. from the suit premises removing all obstruction and for khas possession.

(2) That through inadvertence the suit has been filed in S.C.C. Jurisdiction although the matter in issue involved warrants for the adjudication of the same in a title suit and as such it is necessary for ends of justice and proper adjudication of the suit the S.C.C. 11/72 way kindly be transferred into a regular Title Suit otherwise the plffs. shall be highly prejudiced and shall suffer irreparable loss." On this application dated 10-9-73 the learned S.C.C. Judge passed an order in the following terms:

“বাদী ও বিবাদী হাজিরা দিয়াছেন। কিছু কথা বার্তার পর বাদীগণ এই মকদ্দমা সর্ত্তের মোকদ্দমাতে transfer করার জন্য প্রার্থনা করেছেন। প্রতিলিপি দেওয়া হয়েছে। উভয় পক্ষকে শুনা গেল।

বিবাদী পক্ষ থেকে কোনরুপ আপত্তি উত্তাপন করা হয়নি। ন্যায়ের খাতিরে প্রার্থনা মঞ্জুর। উক্ত মোকদ্দমাকে এস সি সি ফাইল থেকে স্থানান্তর করে সত্ব ফাইলে নেওয়া হোক। ঐ মর্মে সংশিষ্ঠ রেজিস্ট্রী ও আরজী সংশোধিত হোক। বর্তমান দরখাস্তকে আরজির অংশ গন্য করা হোক।

সংশ্লিষ্ট অবস্থা পরিবর্তনের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে আগামী ৭-৩-৭৩ তারিখে বিবাদী পক্ষকে কোনরুপ আপত্তি ও প্রতিকার নেওয়া থাকলে তা নিতে বলা গেল। মোকদ্দমার বিবাদী এখানে উপস্থিত হওয়ায় থাকায় নতুন করে সমনাদি দেওয়ার দরকার নাই। মোকদ্দমা পি লিষ্ট নামিয়ে নেওয়া হোক।”

This is one of the orders challenged in the instant Rule. Mr. M.A. Matin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that the transfer of the S.C.C. Suit to a Title Suit was without jurisdiction in as much as the learned S.C.C. Judge had no jurisdiction to wake a transfer. According to the learned Advocate, the learned S.C.C. Ridge should have returned the plaint under section 23 of the S.C.C. Act which runs as follows:

"23(1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this Act, when the right of a plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a Court of Small Causes depend upon the proof or disproof of a title to immovable property or other title which such a Court cannot finally determine, the Court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a Court having jurisdiction to determine the title.

(2) When a Court returns a plaint under sub-section (1), it shall comply with the provisions of the section paragraph of section 57 of the Code of Civil Procedure (1882) and make such order with respect to costs as it deems just and the court shall, for the purposes of the Indian Limitation Act, 1877, be deemed to have been unable to entertain the suit by reasons of a cause of a nature like to that of defect of jurisdiction."

5. Mr. Matin, construing section 23(1) contends that the application discloses that "the matter in issue involved warrants for the adjudication of the same in a Title suit." This is clearly an indication that the plaintiffs claim the relief upon "proof or disproof of a title to immovable properly or other title which such a court cannot finally determine". Thus according to Mr. Matin the suit is one for title depending on proof or disproof of a title to immovable property which the Small Cause Court cannot finally determine and the learned S.C.C. Judge acted without jurisdiction in transferring the suit from the S.C.C. file to the Title File. The plaintiffs, in paragraph 14(a) of the plaint, stated the relief claimed in the suit in the following terms:

"Evicting the defdt. from the premises described in the schedule below by removing all obstructions and for recovery of khas possession."

<u>6. This prayer discloses that the plaintiffs do not pray for a declaration of their title. A suit for ejectment of the defendant by removing obstructions and for recovery of khas possession, in all circumstances may not depend on a question of proof or disproof of a Title to the immovable properly. In the instant case the plaintiffs do not appear to have claimed the relief depending on proof or dis-proof of a title to the immovable properly. Mr. Matin submits that in a suit under the S.C.C. jurisdiction, the Court may enquire into the question of title. The learned Advocate has referred to a decision in the case of Dr. Habibur Rahman and another Vs. Md. Mansur reported in 25 D.L.R. (Dacca) 211 in support of the proposition. There is no dispute with the proposition laid therein. Unless the plaintiffs framed the suit for a declaration of title with other necessary consequential reliefs, the mere enquiry into the question of title, will not, by itself, convert the suit into a suit for title depending on proof or disproof of title to immovable properly. The provision in section 23(1) of the S.C.C. Act clearly indicates that the Court had jurisdiction to return the plaint at any stage of the proceeding. This is merely directory and not mandatory. It is evident from the expression "the Court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint". On a perusal of the impugned order, it oboes appear that the defendant raised any objection to the plaintiff's prayer. It was not contended before the learned S.C.C. Judge that the relief claimed in the suit depended on the proof or disproof of title to the immovable property. In the circumstances, the court was rot called upon to direct its attention whether or net the relief claimed in the suit depended upon proof or disproof of title to immovable properly and consequently the court was not required to record any finding in that behalf. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that it was the duty of the court to return the plaint if, in its opinion, the relief claimed by the plaintiffs in a suit depended upon the proof or disproof of a title to immovable property or other title which such a court cannot finally determine. In the instant case the learned Munsif has allowed the application in the interest of justice. The averments made in the application dated 10.9.73 clearly indicate that the suit was filed in S.C.C. jurisdiction through inadvertence and that "the matter in issue involved" warrants for an adjudication of the same in a title suit. From this statement, the relief claimed in 'the suit was not changed. The suit with its relief as contained in paragraph 14 remained as before. Thus the transfer, in the interest of justice, cannot be construed to be an act rot contemplated by the provisions of the S.C.C. Act or that the same was without jurisdiction. It may be pointed out that the learned Munsif in whose court the suit, in the S.C.C. Jurisdiction was filed is the court with ordinary Civil Jurisdiction relating to the case. It could not be pointed out on the strength of any authority that the order complained of was without jurisdiction.</u>

<u>7. Mr. T. Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, supporting the impugned order, referred to a decision in the case of Hari Balu Gaekwad and others Vs. Ganapatrao Lakurijinao Gaekawad and others ILR 38 Bombay at page 190 In that case the plaintiffs sued the defendant for recovery of damages caused by way of removal of bamboos etc. The suit was filed in the Court of Subordinate Judge exercising jurisdiction under the S.C.C. Act. In the case of Hari Balu referred to above the suit was originally filed as an S.C.C. Suit in the Court of a Judge having both the Small Causes Court and regular jurisdiction. As it came out that the right of the plaintiffs and the relief claimed by them depended upon the proof or disproof of a title to immovable property which the Small Cause Court could not finally determine, the Judge acting under the power contained in section 23 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act caused the suit transferred to his file as an ordinary judge. It was held that "There was no substantial irregularity in this. He could hardly return the plaint to be presented to another Judge, because he himself was the Judge having jurisdiction to determine the question of title". Mr. T. Ali, the learned Advocate relying upon this decision submits that this is a mere technical objection without any substance behind it. In the instant suit, the plaint as it stands, does not indicate that the relief claimed in the suit depends upon proof or disproof of title to immovable property. The case of Hari Balu is an authority for the proposition that in a case where the court is vested with the jurisdiction under the S.C.C. Act as well as the ordinary civil jurisdiction, a transfer wider section 23 of the Act does not amount to a substantial irregularly. The case relied upon by Mr. T. Ali supports his contention to some extent. In the instant case as observed earlier, the learned Munsif was exercising ordinary civil jurisdiction as well as the jurisdiction as a Judge under the S.C.C. Act. Thus a return by one hand and receipt by the other, made no substantial departure from the principle contemplated by section 23 of the Act. The two distinct acts were combined to one resultant act namely the transfer. Mr. T. Ali next referred to an un-reported case of Joggeswari Debi VS. Chandi Charm Pramanik appearing in 22 C.W.N. page XLVII (Notes). In this case, for a claim of Rs. 9/- representing the value of Bhagarent, a suit was filed in the court of the Munsif and it was wrongly registered as an S.C.C. Suit. As soon as the mistake was detected, the suit was transferred to the file of the learned Munsif exercising the ordinary jurisdiction. In the instant case the application indica.es that the suit was filed in the S.C.C. Jurisdiction through inadvertence and what was sought to be done was the rectification of the mistake. It, therefore, does not appear that the learned S.C.C. Judge acted illegally or with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in transferring the suit from S.C.C. File to the title file in his court.</u>

8. It appears from the impugned order that it was passed in presence of the defendant. The defendant, however, took no step to challenge the same till the instant rule was issued on 28.1.75. Mr. T. Ali has pointed cut that the Rule so far is it relates to the order dated 10.9.73 is barred by limitation. On an examination of the record it appears so being confronted with the problem of limitation the learned Advocate for the petitioner stated that the order dated 10.9.73 was construed as a provisional order and accordingly no steps was taken to assail the same before the instant rule was issued. In the application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before this court, no statement has been made explaining the delay in filing the revision against the order dated 10.9.73. The explanation offered by Mr. Matin finds no support from the record. In the circumstances the Rule as against the order dated 10.9.73 does not survive the mischief of limitation.

<u>9. The other order under challenge is the order dated 25.7.74. By this order the learned Munsif disposed of the issue No. 4 which is as follows:</u>

<u>"Is the suit properly valued and stamped ?" The learned Munsif has accepted the plaintiff's valuation of Rs. 120/- relying upon certain decisions referred to in the order itself. The relief claimed in the suit as observed earlier, does not indicate that the suit, although transferred to the Title file and numbered as a Title Suit is for a declaration of title with recovery of possession requiring to pay advalorem Court fees on the subject-matter of the suit. Mr. Matin, however, pointed out that by the decree the plaintiff seeks to recover kilts possession of certain immovable property with or without the building standing thereon. According to him this property has an objective standard of valuation and as such advalorem court fees on the market value of the said property was payable by the plaintiffs in the suit. This is a suit for recovery of possession upon eviction of a person whom the plaintiffs do not admit to be a tenant under them and accordingly the claim is within the scope of Article 4 of the Second Schedule to the S.C.C. Act. Matin could not point out under what provision of law advalorem Court fee was required for the suit as it stands.</u>

10. Mr. Matin, at last made a grievance that the suit as framed was not maintainable. This question is not before the Court in the instant rule. The question is yet to be decided by the trial court and it is too early to prejudge the matter. No other question has been raised in the Rule. In the circumstances there is no substance in the contention of Mr. Matin and consequently the rule must be discharged.

The result, therefore, is that the Rule is discharged with costs.

End.

lawyer:
M. A. Karim Petitioner.
Abdul Kuddus Mia with Sk. Nurul Islam —For the opposite parties.
parties:
Abid Ali ------Petitioner. 
Vs
 Maleka Khatoon and others. ------opp. parties
full_judgment:
Nurul Haque Bhuiyan, J.:-This Rule under section 115 of the Code of civil procedure at the instance of the pre-emptor-petitioner is directed against the judgment and order dated 30.4.84 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 7 of 1984 reversing those dated 29.12.83 passed by the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Case No. 230 of 1980 allowing the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

2. The facts leading to this Rule are that C.R. plot No. 404 measuring -14 decimals and C.R. plot No. 400 measuring 13 decimals compressing a raiyati holding at a jama of Tk. 20/-recorded in Chakla Roshnabad Khatian No. 1 of mouza Bishuapur popularly known as Kaptan Bazar within Comilla municipality was originally owned by Munshi Torabuddin Kazi. On his death his heirs sold the entire holding to Hosna Balm by a register kabala dated 2. 6. 34  Ext. A(2). After her purchase Hosna Bairn raised residential construction in the holding. Thereafter she transferred the en-tire C.R. plot No. 404 to her daughter O.P. No. 2 Afia Khatun by a registered kabala dated 9.2.52. Ext. A (1) and delivered possession. She sold also the entire C.R. plot No. 400 to her son Abed Ali the pre-emptor by a registered kabala dated 29.4.54 Ext. 1. O.P. No. 2 Afia Khatun the sister of pre-emptor used to stay with her husband to a different place and therefore the pre-emptor alone used to posses the entire holding comprising of 27 decimals of land and he raised residential constructions in C.R. plot No. 404 the opposite No.2 instituted T.S. No. 62 of 1968 in the said court of Munsif against the petitioner with a prayer for ejectment of the petitioner from C.R. plot No. 404. The suit was decreed on compromise on the basis of a solenama Ext. E. on 21.6.69. In terms of the solenama the O.P. No. 2 would get recovery of 12 decimal of land of C.R. plot No. 404 and the petitioner would get '02 decimal of land in the eastern part of the said plot and he would remove the structures. It was further agreed by the parties in the solenama that O.P. 2 would execute a kabala in favour of the pre-emptor in respect of '02 decimals of case plot No. 404. It was stipulated that if the O. P. No. 2 failed to execute the kabala in respcot of the said '02 decimal of the land petitioner would get the same through court in a suit for specific performance of contract. In terms of the solenama the petitioner removed his structures from 12 decimal land in December, 1970 and continued in possession of '02 decimal of laud of the case plot No. 404. Since O.P. No. 2 did not execute a kabala in terms of the solenama the petitioner instituted T.S. No.91 of 1970 in the said court of Munsif for specific performance of contract against the O.P. No. 2 and got a decree on 29.11.72 but the decree was not pa into execution and he did not get any kabala through court. On 17.4.80 O.Ps. Nos. 1-2 asked the petitioner to remove his structures from the said -02 decimal land of case plot No. 404 in presence of witnesses and on that occasion O.P. No.2 disclosed for the first time that she had sold the case plot No. 404 comprising -14 decimals of land to opposite party No. 1 by a registered kabala. Before this date the petitioner had no knowledge of any such kabala. The petitioner procured certified copy of the kabala and learnt about the transfer in details on 19.7.80 that O.P.2 had sold tie entire case plot No. 404 to her daughter O.P. No. 1 by a kabala dated 5.3.75 at a consideration of Tk. 2500/- and the kabala was registered on 21.4.78 under section 60 of the Registration Act. No notice of the impugned transfer was given to the petitioner who is a co-sharer in the suit holding. Therefore, the petitioner filed an application for pre-emption on 7.8.80 under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act depositing statutory compensation along with consideration of the kabala.

3. The opposite parties 1-2 opposed the application for pre-emption by filing written objection. The case of opposite party No. 1 is that the petitioner has no locus standi to seek pre-emption of the impugned transfer as he is not a co-sharer in the case plot No.404 and that the impugned transfer is pot a sale. The application for pre-emption is barred by limitation as the petitioner had knowledge of the impugned transfer from the time of the transfer. Since the petitioner did not pat the decree obtained in. T.S. No. 91 of 1970 into execution the decree became in executable and the petitioner did not acquire any title in the `02 decimal and or the case plot No. 40 on the basis of the sole decree passed on 21.6.69 in T.S. No. 62 of 1968.

4. The learned Munsif allowed the pre-emption of the findings that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the bolding and he has a right to pre-empt the impugned kabala and that the petitioner had no knowledge of the impugned transfer before 17.4.80 and the application for pre-emption was within time.

5. The learned Additional District judge reversed the decision of the learned Munsif and allowed the appeal on the finding that the petitioner is not co-sharer of the case land arid as such he is not entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala and that the petitioner had knowledge about the purchase and possession of the O.P. No. 1 in the case plot No. 404 from long before 17.4.80. and the application for pre-eruption was barred by limitation. Against the judgment and order of the learned Additional District Judge this Rule has been obtained by the pre-emptor petitioner.

6. Mr. M.A. Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor-petitioner has challenged the correctness of the decision of the learned Additional District Judge in this Rule. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Additional District Judge has misread the evidence of the petitioner to hold the view that the petitioner has admitted that he removed his house from the entire caw plot No. 404 and as such he is not a co-sharer of the case land and in that erroneous view he has erred in applying against the petitioner the principle laid down in the case of S.B. Basirullah Vs. Zahurul Islam 35 D.L.R. (AD) 230 that a co-sharer in the land transferred and not a op-sharer in the tenancy has the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act and in holding that the petitioner is net a co sharer in the case land and as such not entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala, The. learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that although the petitioner did not execute the decree obtained in T.S No. 91 of 1970 and the decree became barred by lime his possession of `02 decimals land of the case plot No. 404 continued in part performance of the contract for sale thereof contained in the solenama will be protected against the parties 1-2 under section 53A of the Transfer of property Act and in that view of the, matter he is a co-sharer of the case land with opposite party No. 1 and as such is entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also submitted that the separation of the jama in favour of opposite party No. 1 having been created subsequent to the impure transfer the learned Additional District Judge has erred in holding that in view of the separation of the jama the petitioner it not a co-sharer in the case land and he has no locus standi to pre-empt the impugned kabala. The last submission of Mr. M.A. Karim is that the learned Additional District Judge has erred in holding that the petitioner had knowledge of the impugned transfer long before 17.4.80 without referring to the evidence of P.W.s. on this point.

7. Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No 1. submits that the learned Additional District Judge has correctly found that the petitioner admitted that he removed his house from the entire case plot No. 404 and as such be is not co-sharer in the case land. In reply to the submission of Mr. M. A. Karim, as to protection of petitioner's possession u/s 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah submits that even if the petitioner is found to be in possession of '02 decimals of the case land and his possession is protected u/s 53A of Transfer of Property Act then also he is not a co-sharer in the case land entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala in as much as he has no paramount title in '02 decimals of the case land. In support of this submission Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah has placed reliance in the case of Muhammad Baklish Vs Ziaullah and others PLD 1971 Bagdadul Jadid 42. Mr. Abdul-Kuddus Miah has next submitted that the learned Additional District Judge has correctly found with reference to evidence on record that the pre-emptor had knowledge of the impugned transfer from long before 17.4.80 and the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation. The learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 has also submitted that the point as to protection under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act having not been raised in the courts below it cannot be raised in this court for the first time.

8. It is evident from the deposition of the petitioner as P.W.1 that in his examination-in-chief he has stated that he got `02 decimal of case plot No. 404 as per the solenama in Title Suit No 62 of 1968, that he constructed his house on this 02 decimal of land and has been residing there and that the remaining -12 decimals or land of the case plot is in possession of his sister O.P. No. 2. The evidence of the petitioner in his cross-examination that he removed his house from plot No. 404 should be read and 'considered with reference to his statement in his examination-in chief and in his pleading where he has categorically stated that he removed his house from `12 decimal of the case plot No. 404 and has been residing on `02 decimals of the case land after constructing house there in terms of the solenama. The statement of the petitioner in his cross-examination that he removed his house from plot No. 404 when read and. considered with his statements in his examination-in-chief and his pleading, it becomes clear that by saying that he removed his house from plot No. 404 he meant that his house from '12 decimals of land of case plot No. 404 in terms of the solenama and not from the entire case plot No. 404. In the case reported in PLD 1971 (13.J)-42 the pre-emptor claimed a superior right of pre-emption on the basis of being a co-sharer in the kabala which was acquired by means of a sale evidenced by mutation. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act was applicable to the said sale but no registered instrument was executed.

<u>9. In the Bagdadul Jadid case the case of Abdul Karim Vs. Fazal Muhammad (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 477; PL.D 1967 (SC) 411 has been considered. In the Supreme Court case it was held that "if the right of pre-emption is a right of substitution then certainly the persons seeking to preempt can be pat into the shoes of the stranger purchaser and exercise all the rights including those to which he be-came entitled under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. There was no reason therefore why the transfer in such circumstances should not be pre-emptible when to hold otherwise would amount to opening the door for fraudulent persons to defeat the law of pre-emption. If the transaction amounts to a sale in fact then not withstanding that it is not in the form prescribed by section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act is not altogether void for the defect is curath by getting a registered document drawn up and registered to perfect the inchoate title of the vendee. This perfection can be insisted upon for there is at any rate an enforceable contract of sale even under the Transfer of Property Act and even such an imperfect transaction will give rise to equities in favour of the buyer". The learned Judges of the Lahore High Court (Raghda-ul-Jadid) quoted the above observations of the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of Pakistan and then held the view that at the direct question before the learned Judges was whether an un-registered sale was pre-emptible or not under the provisions of the Punjab Pre-emption Act the above observations in the said Supreme Court case did not appear to be an authority for the proposition that a vendee under an unregistered sale could be regarded as a co-sharer within the meaning of section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act and that the term co-sharer which is not defined in Punjab Pre-emption Act would mean a person who has a title in the khata from which the sale was made and in that view held that in the absence of registered instrument the pre-emptor did not acquire any valid right or title so as to be deemed a co-sharer to exercise the right of pre-emption under section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act even though the rights acquired by him may be defensible u/s 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.</u>

10. In the present case the question is whether the O.P. No.2 after having entered in-to a contract to sell `02 decimals of land of the case plot to the pre-emptor and she and her transferee O.P. No.1 after having accepted the pre-emptor as a co-sharer by their con-duct can they now deny the pre-emptor as a co-sharer of the case land who being already in possession of `02 decimal of the case land has been continuing his possession therein in terms of the contract contained in the 'solenama' ? The answer is no. The O.Ps. 1-2 are estopped from disputing that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the case land. The term "co-sharer" is neither defined in the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act nor in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the facts and circumstances, I hold the view that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the case land and as such is entitled to pre-empt the impugned kabala and this view of mine finds support in the decision of the case reported in PLD-1967 (SC) 411 noted above. I think the decision of the Supreme Court is an authority for the proposition that the pre-emptor having been in possession as part performance of contract for sale can he deemed to be a co-sharer for the purpose of pre-emption. The learned Judges of the Lahore High Court (B.J.) have not fully appreciated the decision of the Supreme Court. Moreover, the question in the present case is not the same as was in the B.J. Case. There the question was whether a pre-emptor claiming as a superior right of pre-emption on the basis of being a co-sharer on the khata acquired by means of sale evidenced by mutation acquired valid right or title in the absence of registration a of the sate under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and could be deemed to be a co-sharer to exercise the right of pre-emption under section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act. The vendor of the pre-emptor in the B.J. Case did not enter into any such contract with the pre-emptor for sale of land as in the present case. Therefore, fact of the present case are distinguishable from those of the B.J. case, and as such the principle laid down in the decision reported in PLD 1971 B.J. 42 is not applicable in the present case. The point as to protection of possession under section 5 3 A of the Transfer of Property Act being a point of law it can be raised in this court though the same was not raised in the courts below. The petitioner having been held to be a co-sharer in the case land the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 wherein it is held that a co sharer in the land transferred and not a co sharer in the tenancy is entitled to preempt under section 24 of the East Bangal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is in favour of the petitioner and the learned Additional District Judge has therefore erred in applying the principle of the said case against the petitioner. The separation of jama in favour of the opposite party No. 1 having been created subsequent to the impugned transfer, the separation in favour of the opposite party No. 1 can not affect the petitioner's right to pre-emption. Therefore, I fully agree with the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the learned Additional District Judge has erred in holding that in view of the separation of the lama the petitioner is not a co-sharer in the case land and has no locus-standi to pre-empt the impugned kabala. As to knowledge of the impugned transfer it may be stated that it is the consistent case of the petitioner in his evidence and pleading that he came to know of the impugned transfer for the first time on 17.4.80. In support of his case he has examined himself and two other witnesses. On proper assessment and consideration of the evidence on record the learned Munsif has come to the conclusion that the petitioner had no knowledge of the transfer on 17.4.80.

12. The learned District Judge has neither discussed the evidence adduced by the petitioner in support of his case nor has he adverted to the reasons given by the learned Munsif in coming to his finding on this point. The learned Additional District Judge has solely relied on the certificate copy of written statement Ext. M on this point. In the said written statement filed on the T.S. No. 566/79 the petitioner stated that he and opposite parties 1-2 (defdts the T.S. No. 566/79) were in ownership and possession of C.R. Plot No. 400 and 404 but there being nothing in the written statement to show that the fact of the impugned transfer was disclosed to the petitioner (in which case C.P. 2 would not be a party) as correctly noted by the learned Munsif, the learned Judge has misread the Ext. `M' to hold the view that the petitioner had knowledge of the impugned transfer from long before 17.4.80. The finding of the learned Additional District Judge that the application is barred by limitation is not therefore tenable and he has wrongly reversed the finding of the learned Munsif on this point. In the circumstances, the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner are of substance and those of the learned advocate for the O.P. No. 1 have no substance. It has already been noticed that the learned Additional District Judge has committed errors of law in deciding the question of co-sharership and of the knowledge of the impugned transfer and the same has led miscarriage of justice.

For the reasons stated above, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the impugned judgment and order of the learned Additional District Judge are set aside and those of the learned Munsif restored.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J: The defendants have filed this petition for leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated the 23rd day of January, 2013 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2512 of 2008 discharging the Rule. 

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the leave petition are that respondent No.1, herein, as plaintiff filed Partition Suit No.51 of 1987 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 1 Court, Chittagong for partition of the suit land. 

3. In the plaint, the plaintiff claimed that he purchased 5(five) decimals land from two plots being RS Plot Nos.2864 and 2861 by registered kabala dated 11.02.1980 from defendant No.9, Roushan Akhter Begum. Though he purchased 5(five) decimals land from two plots, the vendor delivered possession of the transferred land from plot No.2864 only, because the entire land of RS Plot No.2861 "was found to have been given in possession of other purchasers" and since purchase, the plaintiff has been in possession of Plot No.2861. After purchase, the plaintiff constructed a pucca boundary wall on south, possession of which was delivered to him by defendant No.9, but the 3(three) other sides were well demarcated by the CDA road. Defendant Nos.1-4 alleged to have purchased 51/2 decimals land equivalent to 2 gondas and 3 karas of RS Plot Nos.2861 and 2864 from defendant No.9 vide registered sale deeds dated 02.08.1980, 28.08.1980 and 10.10.1980 and took possession of some land on south of the plaintiffs pucca boundary wall. The defendants also claim that they are entitled to get 7' and 5" land on north of the southern pucca wall of the plaintiff wherein the plaintiff is creating disturbance in their possession, for which they filed Other Suit No.16 of 1987 in the Court of Sadar Munsif for permanent injunction which was decreed exparte. Defendant No.9 sold her entire land to the plaintiff and defendant Nos.5-7, there was no land left, but defendant Nos.1-4 taking the advantage that there was no partition of the land by metes and bounds among the co-share purchasers and the order of temporary of injunction restraining the plaintiff from making any construction on his purchased land proceeding with the construction of a multi-storied building on the south of the pucca boundary wall of the plaintiff. Mohd. Faiz Ahmed, husband of defendant No.9 being an employee of CDA fraudulently gave possession of the acquired land of RS Plot No.2864, but on actual measurement, it is found that the plaintiff would get the balance land of RS Plot No.2864, since no other land was left out. The plaintiff requested the defendants to make survey of the suit land, but they are proceeding with the construction works on the basis of the decree obtained in the suit for permanent injunction and hence the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit. 

4. Defendant Nos.1 to 3 and 5 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff purchased 21/2 gonads land with specific boundary from defendant No.9 by registered kabala dated 12.02.1980 and to the south of the land of the plaintiff, the defendants have got a vacant land measuring 7' and 6" running north to south and to the south of this vacant land, the defendants constructed building with some vacant land. The defendants purchased 3 gondas land by registered sale deeds dated 02.08.1980, 28.08.1980, 16.10.1980 and 11.06.1987 from defendant No.9, Roushan Akhter Begum. After their purchase, the defendants made pucca construction on their purchased land and started multi-storied building for the purpose of market demolishing the kachha structures at which the plaintiff raised objection, whereupon defendant Nos.1 to 4 filed Other Suit No.16 of 1987 for permanent injunction and obtained an order of temporary injunction which was violated by the plaintiff and then the defendants prayed for mandatory injunction. 

5. The trial Court by its judgment and decree dated 23.04.2006 decreed the suit in preliminary form giving saham to the plaintiff to the extent of 5 (five) decimals land from the scheduled land, i.e. from the two RS Plots being Nos.2864 and 2861 of RS Khatian Nos.120 and 48 respectively and also gave separate saham to the contesting defendants to the extent of 6(six) decimals land. 

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the plaintiff filed Other Appeal No.302 of 2006 before the District Judge, Chittagong. The learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong by the judgment and decree dated 16.03.2008 allowed the appeal and gave saham to the plaintiff for 5(five) decimals land from RS Plot No.2864 only. The appellate Court also gave saham to the-defendants for 6(six) decimals land purchased by them along with 1(one) decimals land from Plot No.2864. Against the judgment and decree of the appellate Court, the defendant-petitioners preferred Civil Revision No.2512 of 2008 before the High Court Division and a learned Judge of the Single Bench by the impugned judgment and order discharged the Rule. 

7. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners, by referring to the prayer made in the plaint and the schedule thereto, has submitted that the plaintiff prayed for saham for 5(five) decimals land out of the suit land being RS Plot Nos.2864 and 2861, but the appellate Court erroneously gave saham to the plaintiff from RS Plot No.2864 only and the High Court Division also failed to consider the said factual aspect of the case and thus erred in law in affirming the judgment and decree of the appellate Court and as such, the impugned judgment and order calls for interference by this Court by giving leave. 

8. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel, entering caveat on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order. 

9. We have perused the plaint, the judgment and decrees of the Courts below and the impugned judgment and order. 

10. From the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff has made categorical assertion therein that though defendant No.9 sold 21/2 gonads land (equivalent to 5 decimals) to him by registered kabala dated 11.02.1980 out of RS Plot No.2864 of RS Khatian No.120 and RS Plot No.2861 of RS Khatian No.48, gave possession of the transferred land in RS Plot No.2684 only, as the entire land of RS Plot No.2861 "was found to have been given in possession of other purchasers" and the plaintiff has been in possession of said 5(five) decimals of land in RS Plot No.2864. The appellate Court, being the last Court of fact on consideration of the evidence on record and the admitted case of the parties, found that the total area of land in RS Plot No.2864 is 26 decimals, out of that, though the defendant No.9 sold 21/2 gonads land to the plaintiff by registered kabala dated 11.02.1980, 20 decimals land of Plot No.2864 along with the entire land of RS Plot No.2861 was acquired by defendant No.10. After acquisition only 6(six) decimals remained in RS Plot No.2864, out of this, the plaintiff claimed 5(five) decimals land and defendant No.1 claimed only 1(one) decimal land. The appellate Court further found that DWI Daulatur Rahman Chowdhury in his cross-examination clearly admitted the said fact. The appellate Court concluded that the plaintiff is in possession of his purchased 5(five) decimals land amicably and accordingly, allowed the appeal giving saham to him of 5(five) decimals land from RS Plot No.2864 and also gave saham to the contesting defendants to the extent of 1(one) decimal from Plot No.2864 +6(six) decimals of their purchased land. The High Court Division while maintaining the decision of the appellate Court noticed that defendant No.1 examined as DW 1 admitted that “২৮৬৪ দাগের আমাদের খরিদা জমির উত্তর প্রান্তে অবস্থিত। আর.এস নির্মাণ করিয়া তাহার অংশ বাদী দেওয়াল নির্মাণ করেন।” It further appears that the trial Court also gave finding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his possession in the suit land and that finding of possession obviously can be related to his possession in Plot No.2864, as the plaintiff never claimed that he got possession in Plot No.2861, it gave saham from two plots when admittedly, there is no land of the transferor (defendant No.9) in Plot No.2861. 

11. In view of the above, we find nothing wrong with the judgment and order of the High Court Division calling for interference by this Court. We find no merit in the leave petition. 

12. Accordingly, the same is dismissed. 

End.

lawyer:
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate instructed by Bivash Chandra Biswas, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the petitioner
