case_source:
(From the judgment and order dated the 2nd day of August, 2017 passed by the 
High Court Division in writ petition No. 2122 of 2016)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali, J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed a against the judgment and order dated 02.08.2017 passed by the High Court Division in writ petition No. 2122 of 2016 discharging the Rule Nisi.

2. The facts, relevant for disposal of the case in brief, are that the writ-petitioner is an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and is one of the owners of plot No. 50 (Gulsan South Commercial Area). The writ-petitioner previously filed writ petition No 6155 of 2004 challenging the allotment letter dated 01.11.2004 issued by RAJUK having allotted 3 kathas, 5 chhataks land adjacent to plot No. 50. The High Court Division by judgment and order dated 31.08.2005 disposed of the Rule Nisi with certain observations. Civil petition for leave to appeal No. 1483 of 2005 was filed by present respondent No. 8 against the judgment dated 31.08.2005, but the same was dismissed. Civil Review petition No. 76 of 2008 was filed, but that was also dismissed as barred by limitation. It is alleged that writ-respondents, despite the judgment of the High Court Division and this Division, allotted 1 katah 12 chhatak of land creating plot No. 33 (A), to the silver Line Associate (writ respondent No.8) by order dated 21.09.2005 and entered into a lease deed on the same date. The write-respondent also approved the plan by the memo dated 23.09.2013 for constructing a multi level car park on the said plot No. 33(A) which will obstruct the access to the writ-petitioner as well as other to enter plot No. 50 from Road No. 133. Hence the writ-petitioner filed writ petition No. 2122 of 2016 and obtained the Rule Nisi.

3. Writ-respondent No. 8 contested the Rule Nisi by filling affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that earlier writ-respondent No. 8 was allotted 3 kathas 5 chhatak 15 square feet land in plot No. 33 (A), situated on the west side of Road No. 133, adjacent to the back side or plot Nos. 50, 52, 33 and 6 contained in commercial layout plan of Gulshan South Commercial Area, Gulshan vide sanction letter dated 01.11.2004 pursuant to a decision taken in Meeting No. 06/2004 of RAJUK held on 05.08.2004, subsequently, in compliance of the direction given in Writ Petition No. 6155 of 2004 given on 31.08.2005, as affirmed by the appellate Division, RAJUK modified the said allotment and allotted 1 katha 8 chahatacks of the land remaining in plot No. 33 (A) as the pathway known as continuation of Road No. 133 which ends at the building of writ-petitioner situated in plot No. 50. Thus it does not in any way create any obstruction/hindrance to access the write-petitioner's building in plot No. 50 from road no. 133. It is further stated that the said allotted land measuring 1 katha 12 chhatacks is unused land and there is no reason to create any obstruction thereon to the write-petitioner or others if construction is made as per plan. Hence the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged.

4. In due course, after hearing both the parties, the Rule Nisi was discharged by the impugned judgment and order. Hence, the writ-petitioner filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

5. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the direction given in the earlier judgment dated 31.08.2005 passed in writ petition No. 6155 of 2004 that allotment should be made "excluded the path from the plot of the petitioner leading to Road No. 133 enabling the petitioner to use his garages which were constructed with approval of RAJUK at the back of the house" and not merely by maintaining access to the writ petitioner's plot. Thus the High Court Division failed to consider whether the impugned allotment, lease deed and building plan approval maintained such access to the garges of the writ-petitioner. He further submitted that the High Court Division failed to consider the plan of the ground floor of the petitioner's building as constructed on plot no. 50 showing the location of the garges, and they layout plan showing the location of the newly created plot No. 33A which impeded access from Road No. 133 to the garges of the petitioner and hence the impugned allotment, lease deed and building plan derogated from and defied the earlier judgment dated 31.08.2005 passed in writ petition No. 6155 of 2004 which explicitly directed for such access to be maintained. He further submitted that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the impugned allotment was made without following any transparent process of competitive bidding although the petitioner could have participated having been the owner of the plot adjacent to the proposed plot.

6. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent No. 1 made submission in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.

7. Mr. Shah Monjurul Haque, learned Advocate, on behalf of respondent No. 8 also submission in support of the impugned and order of the High Court Division.

8. We have considered the submission of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned and perused the impugned judgment and other materials on record.

9. From the findings of the High Court Division, it appears that the petitioner in this case is that lessee and as such he is in possession of the plot No. 50, Gulshan Avenue. The said plot is on the corner of Gulshan Avenue and South Avenue and therefore has access from both of those roads. In addition, the said plot has access to the back of the plot through Road No. 133 which is a cul de sac starting from Road No. 134 and ending at plot No. 50. Plot No. 50 is adjacent to plot No. 33 on the eastern side and plot No. 52 on the northern side. There is a small parcel of land in between plot No. 50 and plot No. 33 adjacent to Road No. 133 which has been marked as plot No, 33A and was allotted to the owner of plot No. 52. The petitioner claim that the owner of plot No. 52 upon obtaining allotment of plot No. 33A is making construction on his two plots in such a manner that Road No. 133, which divides plot No. 52 and plot No. 33A is being encroached as a result the petitioner's access to his plot via Road No. 133, is being obstructed.

<u>10. We find from the earlier judgment dated 31.08.2005 passed in writ petition No. 6115 of 2016 that RAJUK was categorically directed to modify its lease in respect of plot No. 33A ensuring that Road No. 133 leading to plot No. 50 of the petitioner is excluded from the lease. In other words, the clear message was that Road No. 133 lading to the petitioner's plot No. 50 would remain as a road for access to that plot. In view of such direction in the earlier writ petition, the High Court Division in the instant writ petition noted as follows: "It is clear from the approved plan that even if construction work is completed on plot No. 33A, the petitioner would have access to plot No. 50. The petitioner can enter plot No. 50 through the front side and also from the back side through Road No. 133.</u>

11. The crux of the petitioner's claim is that he wants access to his plot No. 50 via Road No. 133 to remain intact and apprehends that respondent No. 8, M/S Silver Line Associate, less of plot No. 52 as well as plot No. 33A will make construction connecting the two plots, i.e. plot No. 52 and plot No. 33A, thus blocking the access of the petitioner from Road No. 133.

12. From the maps which have been sup-plied by the petitioner, in particular, the sketch maps appearing at pages 165 and 166 of the present petition, we do not find any connectivity between plot No. 542 and plot No. 33A. These two plots are clearly separated by road no. 133 which ends at the rear boundary of plot No. 50.

13. In view of the above discussion, we find that the petitioner has and will continue to have access to his plot No. 50 by means of Road No. 133 and that no development works shall take place to obstruct Road No. 133 leading to the petitioner's plot.

14. Accordingly, with the above observation, the civil petition for leave to appeal is disposed of.

End.

lawyer:
Sonia Zaman Khan with Md Reajul Hasan Advocates -------- For the Petitioners. 
Dilruba Sharmin, Advocate ------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Estate Management Partners Limited and another --------- Petitioners
vs
Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK) and another --------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J : In this Application under Article 102 of the Constitution, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the Respondents should not be directed to issue transfer permission to the Petitioners to transfer the flats in the building situated at Plot No. CWS(C) 5, Road No. 21, Gulshan-1, Dhaka-1212 as requested by the Petitioners vide letter dated 27-3-2011 (Annexure-'A') on acceptance of transfer fees as fixed by RAJUK and/or pass other or further Order or Orders as to this may seem fit and proper.

2. The Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) [later Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK)] vide its Letter of Allotment being Memo No. DIT/Gulshan-2650 dated 3-4-1962 allotted Plot No. 5, Block-CWS(C) in Gulshan Model Town ("plot") to one Mr SM Hassan, an architect. After getting such allotment, Mr Hassan paid the entire consideration value for the plot as well as the ground rent. Thereafter, Mr Hassan constructed a one-storied building on the plot. In time Mr Hassan applied to DIT for granting permission to transfer the plot to his wife Begum Ummat Rasool by way of gift. Thereafter, DIT vide its Memo No. DIT/ EO/3359 dated 29-7-1970 permitted Mr SM Hassan to transfer the plot to his wife. In the said Memo dated 29-7-1970 it was also stated that after such transfer, the lease deed plot may be registered in favour of Begum Ummat Rasool. Consequentially, RAJUK's predecessor entity DIT executed a Lease Deed on 31-8-1970 leasing out the plot in favour of Begum Ummat Rasool for a period of ninety-nine years. The said Lease Deed was registered as Registered Lease Deed No. 18469-133-25/1970 DACCA on 22-12-1970 before the Office of District Registrar, Dhaka. Thus, Begum Ummat Rasool became the sole owner of the plot.

3. The detailed conditions of the said lease are enumerated in the Lease Deed dated 22-12-1970, Condition 23 of which states that the lessor, i.e., presently RAJUK, has the right to collect transfer fee to enable further transfer of the plot. The Petitioners assert that from a clear reading of Condition 23 it is apparent that the fee payment requirement does not operate to restrict further the transfer of the plot. Rather it confers a right to transfer upon payment of requisite fees to RAJUK. RAJUK's interest is confined to the earning of revenue and facilitating such transfer as a service-provider and its defined role is of collecting the fee by way of a prior charge on the plot. The fee cannot in the circumstance, however, operate as a deterrent or hindrance to the exercise of the right to transfer. Condition 23 reads thus:

"That subject to the provision of condition No.22 of this presents, the lessee shall be at liberty to transfer the whole of the demised property but not any part of it and giving clear 30 days notice to the Lessor and on prior payment to Lessor of a transfer fee which shall constitute a prior charge on the demised property and which for all transfer taking places before the first day of January 1971 shall be at the rate of Rs.1000 per bigha of the demised property and for transfer taking place thereafter shall be at a rate to be fixed by the Lessor after that date;

Provided that in cases of gift to husband, wife or children or grand children, no transfer fee shall be payable; Provided further that no transfer fee shall be payable for a transfer in the shape of a mortgage, unless the mortgagee exercises his right of foreclosure on the property if sold in execution of a decree of a Civil Court for the mortgage, money or for any debt of the Lessee purchased by a person other than the Lessee;

Provided further that in all cases of transfer the Lessor shall have the right of pre-emption."

4. As sole owner of the plot Begum Ummat Rasool leased out the building thereon in favour of Adamjee Jute Mills Limited for a monthly rent of Rs. 1,200 commencing from 1-2-1970. Thereafter, Begum Ummat Rasool entered into an Agreement for Sale on 28-9-1971 with the Petitioner No. 2, Mr Shamsul Haque with regard to the plot at a consideration of Rs. 1,17,300 out of which a sum of Rs. 25,000 was paid by Mr Haque as advance payment. It was also agreed that Mr Haque would have to pay the rest of the consideration value within two months effective from obtaining the necessary transfer approvals from DIT and others. The Agreement for Sale was registered as Registered Deed of Agreement for Sale No. 7577 before the Office of District Registrar, Dhaka.

5. After entering into the Agreement for Sale, Begum Ummat Rasool executed a registered Special Power of Attorney, being Special Power of Attorney No. 7578 dated 28-9-1971, appointing her husband Mr Hassan as her true and lawful attorney to receive the balance amount of the consideration value, to give receipt and to take any other steps in connection with the plot on her behalf.

6. Begum Ummat Rasool having applied to DIT on 29-9-1971 for transfer permission, DIT vide its Memo No. DIT/EO/1215 dated 20-1-1971 granted such transfer permission subject to conditionalities as were eventually fulfilled leading DIT to issue its Memo No. DIT/ EO/1233 dated 22-10-1971 permitting Begum Ummat Rasool to transfer the plot to Mr Haque in the following terms:

"That you are permitted to execute and registered deed of transfer of the plot in favour of Mr Shamsul Hoque, SO Late Moulvi Hazrat Ali of Vill-Malapdia, PS Serajdikhan, Dist. Dacca before the District Registrar, Dacca, mentioning therein the consideration amount of Rs 1,20,000 (Rupees one lac and twenty thousand) only which you have mentioned in your letter".

It is asserted that Mr Haque has since been in peaceful possession of the plot and also occupying the residential building thereon.

7. It so transpired that thereafter Mr Haque on several occasions requested Begum Ummat Rasool and her constituted attorney Mr Hassan to execute and register a sale deed pertaining to the plot upon receiving the balance consideration amount, but to no avail. Neither Begum Ummat Rasool nor her constituted attorney took any step in this regard. Accordingly, Mr, Haque, as plaintiff, filed a suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 85 of 1972 before the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka impleading Begum Ummat Rasool, Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works as defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Mr Haque prayed inter alia for alternate reliefs thus:

"(a) For passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff for specific performance of contract, and also for execution and registration of the Sale Deed for Rs. 1,17,300 with respect to the suit property v described in the schedule of the plaint.

(b) For causing such a Kabala executed and registered through Court, in case the defendant does not do so in pursuance of the decree within the time to be allowed by this Court."

The First Court of Sub-ordinate Judge vide judgment and decree dated 27-5-1974 decreed the suit in favour of Mr Haque and against the defendant No. 3 on contest and against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 ex parte. Rejecting the Government's contention that the suit is barred by the provisions of President's Order No. 16 of 1972, the Court found for Mr Haque given that his purchase of the suit plot predated PO 16 of 1972 and the plot had been in Mr Plaque's possession since. The operative part of the judgment reads thus:

"that the suit be and is decreed on contest against the contesting defendant No. 3 and ex-parte against the rest. The deft No. 1 is directed to execute and register a sale deed in respect of the suit property as described in the plaint schedule in favour of the plff within 30 days from this day on receipt of the balance consideration amount of Taka 95,000 from the plff and in default the plff shall get the same so effected and registered through the Court by depositing the balance consideration amount of Taka 95,000 in the credit of the deft No. 1 after the expiry of 30 days from this day at the cost of the plff. The plff is entitled to withdraw from Court such sum to Taka as may be required for obtaining the Income Tax Clearance and Capital Gain Tax certificate."

8. The Government as defendant No. 2 preferred First Appeal No.241 of 1974 against the judgment and decree of 27-5-1974 before the High Court Division which by its Order dated 11-5-1983 dismissed the appeal for default of the appellant.

9. It so transpired that Begum Ummat Rasool took no steps to complete the transfer of the plot even after the expiry of the thirty-day period specified in the judgment and decree dated 27-5-1974. Accordingly, as per the dispensation in the said judgment Mr Haque deposited Taka 95,000 in the First Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka by way of Government Challan No.3734 dated 18-11-1974. Thereafter, Mr Haque filed Title Execution Case No. 42 of 1974 before the said Court for having the sale deed executed and registered through Court further to which the Court executed Sale Deed No. 395 dated 28-12-1974 as was registered before the Office of District Registrar, Dhaka for and on behalf of Begum Ummat Rasool, thereby, effectively transferring the plot to Mr Haque. Mr Haque's application to RAJUK's predecessor entity DIT followed thereafter for mutating his name with regard to the plot in the record of rights. Even though Mr Haque enclosed the certified copy of the judgment, the registered Sale Deed dated 28-12-1974 and other relevant documents, DIT vide its Memo No. DIT/EO/1088 dated 8-3-1977 declined to mutate his name citing the reason that DIT was not made a party in Title Suit No. 85 of 1972. In the meantime, Mr Haque got his name mutated with all other departments like the City Corporation, various utility service-providers, the Settlement Department etc. in connection with the plot. He also got his name mutated with the Gulshan Revenue Office and obtained Mutation Khatian dated 8-5-1976. It is asserted that the Gulshan Revenue Office also issued a Field Survey Khatian on 30-5-1999 in Mr Haque's favour in connection with the said plot.

10. Eventually, Mr Haque filed an appeal before the Chairman, DIT against DIT's decision not to mutate his name. This significantly led to DIT vide Memo No.DIT/ EO/1399-L dated 11-4-1978 directing Mr Haque to deposit the sum of Taka 2,887.50 as transfer fee coupled with Taka 1,872 interest for mutating his name. Mr Haque, accordingly, deposited the transfer fee with interest to DIT which vide Memo No.DIT/E0/1517-L dated 26-4-1978 informed him that his name had been mutated in DIT's records in respect of the plot in the terms below:

"With reference to your letter dated 17-4-78 and certified copy of transfer deed No. 395 dated 6-1-75, the undersigned is directed to inform you that name and records in respect of plot No. CWS(C) 5 and the house constructed thereon at Gulshan have been mutated in your favour. Henceforth, you will be treated as lessee of the Dacca Improvement Trust."

The Petitioners submit that DIT, thereby, vide the said Memo dated 26-4-1978 accepted Mr Haque's valid title and interest in the plot in keeping with the earlier judicial verdict. This has resulted in Mr Haque being placed in the shoes of the original lessee, i.e., Begum Ummat Rasool. Predicated on that argument the Petitioners submit that DIT, and consequentially RAJUK, have accepted Mr Haque as a lessee and he having not violated any term of the lease is entitled to a sale permission to be granted him as and when he requests the same of RAJUK. The Petitioners reiterate that both DIT and RAJUK from time to time variously issued the requisite permissions to mortgage the property and to appoint a constituted attorney and finally approved the construction plan for a six-storied building on the plot, thereby, displaying a consistent pattern of favourable decisions not only ensuring to the benefit of Mr Haque's proprietary interests in the land but also for furtherance of such interests within legal bounds. It follows, therefore, that Mr Haque, against whom no allegation was ever brought for violating any plot lease terms, has had a right accrued to him to a permission to sell the apartments constructed thereon with a concomitant legal obligation devolving on RAJUK to issue the same.

11. In evidence of Mr Haque's regular dealings in the plot as further fortified his present claim before this Court, it is noted that upon Mr Haque's application of 20-7-1985. DIT vide Memo No. DIT/Estate /2008 dated 3-8-1985 accorded him permission to obtain a secured loan from Uttara Bank Limited by mortgaging the plot. Mr Haque eventually repaid the entire loan amount and redeemed his mortgage as evident in a series of documents relating to the return of his property documents by Uttara Bank vide Memo No. UBL/LO/SD/2005/378 dated 27-7-2005, Mr Haque's acknowledgement of receipt of the same dated 28-7-2005 and he informing RAJUK vide letter dated 4-9-2005 that the plot has been released from the mortgage earlier created in favour of Uttara Bank.

12. As part of a continuous chain of transactions furthering his interest in the plot without let or hindrance, in due course, Mr Haque entered into a land development agreement with the Petitioner No. 1, Estate Management Partners Limited ("EMPL") on 6-2-2006 for constructing a six-storied building and to that end executed an Irrevocable Power of Attorney ("PoA") dated 6-2-2006 appointing EMPL's Managing Director as his duly constituted Attorney for construction and other attendant and ancillary purposes. Notably, RAJUK vide Memo dated 5-9-2006 accepted and approved the PoA upon satisfaction of all its terms inclusive of prospective sale of eight apartments by the Attorney. This is amply manifested in RAJUK's Memo dated 5-9-2006 granting permission for such sale.

13. Clause 3 of the PoA endorses the Attorney's authority to deal in the eight apartments out of twenty thus:

"3. To sell, transfer, exchange, allot and dispose of 8 (eight) apartments and 8 (eight) car parks out of 20 (twenty) Apartments and 20 (twenty) car parks undivided and undetached shares or portions of the Scheduled Land to the buyers at a price to be determined by the Developer as attorney and receive money from the buyers and give receipts to the same and to execute the above mentioned documents."

The Petitioners strenuously argue that RAJUK having considered the said Clause 3 mechanism of transference of possessory and proprietary interest in accepting and approving the PoA as it did on 5-9-2006, also concomitantly recognized the centrality of the transfer mechanism explicit in Clause 3 for the effective conveyance of the said eight apartments. The relevant part of the said Memo dated 5-9-2006 is quoted below:

“বিষয় ও সূত্রোল্লিখিত আবেদনের প্রেক্ষিতে নিম্নস্বাক্ষরকারী আদিষ্ট হইয়া আপনাকে জানাইতেছেন যে, আপনার কর্তৃক সম্পাদিত আম-মোক্তারনামা দলিল নং ১৯০৫/২০০৬ তারিখ ৬-২-২০০৬ ইংরেজি বলে গুলশান আবাসিক এলাকায় সিডব্লিউএস(সি) ব্লকের ৫ নং প্লটটির ব্যাপারে হস্তাত্তর দলিল রেজিষ্ট্রীকরণসহ আম-মোক্তারনামায় বর্ণিত যাবতীয় কার্যক্রম আপনার পক্ষে সম্পন্ন ও সম্পাদন করার জন্য এষ্ট্রেট ম্যানেজমেন্ট পার্টনার লিঃ এর পক্ষে উহার ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক জনাব তসলিম মোঃ খান, ঠিকানাঃ বাড়ী ৯, রোড: ৮, ধানমন্ডি, ঢাকা ১২০৫ কে অনুমতি প্রদান করা হইল । এখানে উল্লেখ্য যে, নিযুক্ত আম-মোক্তার বর্ণিত প্রট/ফ্ল্যাট তার পরিবারের কোন সদস্যকে দান/হেবা করতে পারবে না।”

In the meantime, RAJUK vide its Memo No. রাজউক/এষ্টট/৫৫৮৮ dated 24-8-2006 had notably directed Mr Haque to deposit the service charge in respect of the plot to the amount of Taka 21,207 due for the period from 1-1-1981 to 31-12-2006. This was complied with by Mr Haque without undue delay.

14. Predicated on the above, Mr Haque progressed to submitting on 27-8-2006 a building plan of the proposed six-storied building for RAJUK's approval accompanied by the prescribed fee payment. RAJUK vide its Memo No. রাজউক/নকশা/২৭৯২/০৬/১৪৪৯ dated 14-9-2006, consequentially, accorded the required approval to the building plan submitted. The case facts attest to the Petitioners' construction thereafter of a building on the plot. During the period of construction the Office of Sub-Divisional Engineer, Public Works Maintenance Sub-Division No. 2 vide its Memo No. রঃবেঃউঃবিঃ-২/ঢাকা/১৬৩২ dated 27-9-2009 requested the Petitioners to ensure that such construction work does not cause any harm to the adjacent Government property. There is nothing on record to suggest any objection being raised by any quarter subsequently in this regard concerning the construction work in this context.

15. Drawing on the facts as above and highlighting the cumulative substantive consequence of all regulatory approvals variously given by DIT and RAJUK in Mr Haque's favour, the learned Advocate for the Petitioners Ms. Sonia Z Khan submits that both DIT and RAJUK by way of a series of endorsements and approvals recognized at all material times Mr Haque as the plot owner with an inalienable right to effectively transfer his apartments constructed thereon. Arguably, imposed concomitantly is a legal obligation on RAJUK to grant inter alia the permission of transfer on fulfillment of all prerequisites by the Petitioners. Indeed, Ms. Khan argues that RAJUK would now be estopped from denying such entitlement and be held accountable for its procrastination and inertia evident in its failure to grant permission to transfer the said apartments on accepting payment of the requisite transfer fees.

16. In due course, Mr Haque's Constituted Attorney on 24-5-2010 applied to RAJUK for permission to transfer four apartments from within the share of the developer-Constituted Attorney. RAJUK's failure to respond to the same led to yet another application on 27-3-2011 to RAJUK to accord transfer permission to sell out eight apartments falling within the share of the developer-Constituted Attorney. RAJUK, however, continued to sit idle on the applications in an initial display of prevarication, thereby, digressing markedly from the regular and established course of conduct of readily granting all .regulatory approvals in confirmation of Mr Haque's due dealings in his property.

17. Mr Haque's Constituted Attorney persistent efforts at securing a transfer permission from RAJUK upon acceptance of transfer fees proved futile and at one stage in 2011 RAJUK's functionaries informed the Petitioners of the plot's purported inclusion in a list of "(বিতর্কীত properties. On further query such functionaries, however, failed to assign any reason for such inclusion of the plot in the list of ostensible disputed properties failing significantly also to produce any actual list issued by any authority whomsoever in substantiation of their contention. Alerted to something being amiss, by way of abundant caution and prudence Mr Haque requested RAJUK in writing on 24-8-2011 to exclude his property from any such list. That spurred RAJUK to constitute a committee for considering such request for exclusion vide Memo No. রাজউক/এ-১/সিডব্লিউএস(সি)-০৫ dated 14-12-2011.

18. Critical of RAJUK's handling of the Petitioners' interests, they now submit that RAJUK desisted from taking any step to accord transfer permission to Mr Haque despite repeated representations made. This is all the more disconcerting for the Petitioners given their proven track record of compliance with all regulatory requirements eliciting permissions and approvals previously given at all material times. RAJUK's abrupt volte-face now on the issue of transfer permission in the absence of any laches on the Petitioners' part, Ms. Sonia Z Khan submits, does that authority no particular credit. Moreover, the apparent obfuscation of issues (evident in the dubious listing of the property as a "disputed" one) points to a level of administrative obtuseness verging on mala fide, arbitrariness and illegality' meriting redress in judicial review.

19. RAJUK's Affidavit-in-Opposition filed in the face of credible allegations of institutional inertia, indifference and ineptitude bordering on institutional and institutionalized apathy is notably silent on the Petitioners' transgressions, if any, or violation of the law meriting the effective denial of transfer permission complained of in this Writ Petition. Unsurprisingly, therefore, the Affidavit-in-Opposition brings forth no specific denial of the Petitioners' case or title to the case plot. At this juncture, RAJUK's lawyer, Ms. Dilruba Shormin, in a bewildering development, has made a revelation at once incredible, disheartening and worrisome that can only be termed by this Court as a denouement. She candidly admits, short of acknowledging RAJUK's irresponsibility, that the original RAJUK File (Nothi) concerning the plot has inexplicably long gone "missing" and is yet to surface. This, Ms. Shormin would have this Court believe, has been the immediate cause for the plot being placed on the list of "disputed" properties. In this Court's view, and for want of a better explanation from RAJUK, this is a mere pretext for shifting incredibly the onus on the plot owner and EMPL to produce copies of all relevant documents relating to the said plot in proof of allotment to Mr Haque. They having complied with such request, RAJUK, upon collecting the relevant documents from Mr Haque and being prima facie satisfied of their provenance, authenticity and veracity, created a "Loose File " concerning the plot. By way of clarification Ms. Shormin submits that RAJUK, in ostensible good faith and for the allottee's convenience, relying on the "Loose File" accorded Mr Haque permission for developing the land and the PoA executed by him was simultaneously approved.

20. It is evident from the File produced by RAJUK before this Court that during the pendency of the instant Writ Petition RAJUK prepared a so-called "List of Disputed Plots" on 3-2-2014. The File contains a summary of chronological events relating to Mr Haque's plot being No. CWS(C) 5. From the File index it is evident that RAJUK had lost the original file/ records relating to the said plot and caused a General Diary entry to be made on 24-8-2006 apprising the police of such incident. Thereafter, Mr Haque, at RAJUK's insistence, submitted all papers relating to the plot which RAJUK, upon verification and full satisfaction of Mr Haque's title, relied upon and used to reconstitute a "Loose File". Evidently further, the documents supplied by Mr Haque were collated in the "Loose File" with the approval of the concerned authority within RAJUK. Acting on the said reconstituted "Loose File", RAJUK also accorded permission to Mr Haque to deposit the service charges against the said plot on 4-6-2006.

21. Ms. Khan argues, plausibly and satisfactorily, that there being no litigation pending and no one having forwarded to RAJUK or otherwise set up any claim adverse to the right, title and interest of Mr Haque in the plot, the Respondent No. 1, RAJUK had acted without substantiation and, therefore, arbitrarily and wholly without lawful authority in treating the plot as a disputed one. Given such provenance and genesis of the "List of Disputed Plots" as prepared by RAJUK on 3-2-2014, the said List, Ms. Khan submits, cannot operate on any level of credibility to affect the right, title and interest of Mr Haque in the plot given that the List was prepared primarily to recreate and preserve the copies of original papers pertaining to the plot and remedy or cure any laches, lapses and negligence that were wholly internal to RAJUK or of its own making. RAJUK's subsequent action purporting to reopen and reclassify the decided and established issue of Mr Haque's title and interest in the circumstances is submitted by Ms. Khan to be unwarranted, uncalled for, arbitrary, tainted with malice and, therefore, illegal and without any legal effect.

22. In substantively disposing of the Rule against such factual backdrop and the attendant issues, this Court finds at the outset that an extract from the reconstructed RAJUK administrative "Loose File" placed before this Court attests to all the factual assertions and developments as averred in the main Writ Petition. How, therefore, is RAJUK's inertia in releasing a transfer permission to be viewed in that context? In a case as this, it is invariably prudent for the parties concerned and the Court sitting on judicial review to be reminded primarily of the nature of the administrative authority being exercised in the facts and the manner indeed in which the power to decide on issues touching on the rights of the citizenry ought to be exercised. The classic assertions of Lord Reid in Ridge vs Baldwin reported in 119631 2 All ER 66 (HL) on the nature and extent of administrative powers presents itself to this Court to be the deciding element in this case. It is a legal truism that administrative authorities in arriving at decisions that impact upon the rights and interests of individuals operate in a 'judicial' or 'quasi judicial' capacity. The precise connotation of such terminology and their usage in the realm of administrative law was succinctly spelt out in cases like Ridge vs Baldwin and, for example, Mc lanes vs Onslow-Fane reported in 11978] 3 All ER 211. Lord Reid maintained that the word 'judicial' had until the 1960s been misconstrued as being possessed of characteristics over and above the characteristic that such power affected a person's rights. He stressed the fact that the power which affects persons rights and interests must be exercised judicially i.e., fairly. It is deduced from Lord Reid's observations, therefore, that when the power exercised is purely administrative as opposed to being purely judicial, it does not make it any less judicial if its exercise affects rights of a person. Further content to that dictum in Ridge vs Baldwin was provided by Megarry V-C in Mc lnnes vs Onslow-Fane when he expressed a preference in such circumstances to highlight the elements of 'fairness' or 'duty to act fairly' in preference to the word 'justice' when any administrative decision, action or even inaction potentially curbs the entrenched rights of an individual. As, therefore, Sedley J emphatically asserted in R vs Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food ex P. Humble Offshore Fisheries Ltd. reported in 09951 2 All ER 714. " the real question is one of fairness in public administration." (See, Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, "Certiorari: An Administrative Law Remedy" Mullick Brothers, 2011 see pages 69-75).

23. It is in that light that this Court has had to examine the sufficiency of the submissions brought forth by the Petitioners' learned Advocate Ms. Sonia Z. Khan on the manner in which the rights of the Petitioners have been trampled upon by the impugned inaction of RAJUK, in particular.

<u>24. The Petitioner's learned Advocate has argued on the long held and tested position in administrative law that prescribes fetters being placed on the exercise of discretionary power and that, resultantly, any such power unreasonably and arbitrarily exercised without proper application of mind shall be found to be unsustainable in law (Lutfu Mia vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 105.) She has also relied on the ratio decidendi in Raj Kumar Behani vs Banglad6h reported in 15 BLD 633 as substantiates our finding in the instant case that RAJUK's inaction amounting to a restriction imposed on the right to transfer is not by way of any sanction of law and, therefore, must be found to have been exercised in a manner as is violative of the right guaranteed under Article 31 of the Constitution and that, furthermore, in the facts there being no efficacious alternative remedy the Petitioners have rightfully invoked the judicial review provisions of the Constitution.</u>

25. In that regard, this Court finds the Raj Kumar Behani Case to be authority for the view that refusal and/or intransigence of any administrative authority of doing that which is otherwise not prohibited under the law but is rather incumbent upon it to execute in the interest of the duty to act fairly and reasonably cannot in any way create a legal presumption of a rightful curbing of the proprietary rights of any citizen.

In that regard the Court in Raj Kumar Behani Case held thus at paragraph 9, at page 636:

"In the above said case it was held that restrictions imposed to the rights of the citizen in contravention of the fundamental right being discriminatory guaranteed under the Constitution and in presence of those restrictions the registering authority refused to accept the sale deed for registration was found to have been' made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. In the instant case we have already found that the restriction imposed are not by way of any promulgation of law but it is done by way of administrative order. Here we are not to find out the reasonableness or otherwise of the order, we are to see only whether this order has the sanction of law. The order having imposed restriction on the right of the petitioner to transfer or otherwise to dispose of his property to another also on the right of the citizen of Bangladesh to acquire property is discriminatory and also violative of the fundamental right guaranteed under the Constitution and the equality clause provided under Article 31."

That being the case, and this Court being satisfied of the adequacy of submissions made on the Petitioners' behalf, it is found that the Petitioners having fulfilled all conditions imposed at all material times without any objection raised by the RAJUK [Imam Dockyard vs RAJUK reported in 2 BLC 202], there can be no reasonable justification for the continued inertia in dealing with the Petitioners' request for permission to transfer on acceptance of the requisite transfer fee. This Court holds that the requirement of payment of the requisite fee is not to be read as a restriction on the proprietary rights of any individual as the Petitioner No. 2, Mr Haque that encapsulates the right to transfer, sell etc. Rather, such requirement of a fiscal exaction is to be read as a facilitator for full enjoyment of all rights attendant upon ownership and possessory rights ensuring to an individual's benefit and which cannot be curbed, denied or in any way be held in abeyance at RAJUK's sweet will and discretion without any sanction of law. Rather, the presumption will be, and this Court expressly finds to that effect, that fairness in discharge of a public duty demands of RAJUK to operate with transparency and without impunity to extend all possible assistance and grant all approvals to a property owner as the Petitioner No. 2 to maximize his guaranteed right to enjoy his property as permitted by law. RAJUK is in that context found to have fallen short of such exacting standards of administration and public service, thereby, entitling the Petitioners to the relief claimed for. The sudden surfacing of a "List of Disputed Plots " and the loss of the original plot file are all indicative further of devices hatched to defeat the interests of citizens like the Petitioner No. 2, Mr Haque. This case has permitted this Court to take a peek into the inner workings of RAJUK and the picture that emerges is hardly complimentary. It is one of opaque decision-making processes embarked upon for collateral purpose which when challenged before the Courts fail to elicit any plausible explanation from RAJUK. We are convinced, therefore, of an absence of any plausible reason or legal justification for RAJUK's continued denial to Mr Haque of a transfer permission that in the facts is rightfully his due.

26. Predicated on the above, the Respondent No. 1, RAJUK is, hereby, directed to issue the necessary transfer permission in clear and express terms in keeping with the Petitioners' application dated 27-3-2011 (Annexure-'A') within a period not exceeding 3 (three) months computed from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order.

27. In the result, the Rule Nisi is made absolute with the direction above.

28. There is no Order as to costs.

Communicate this Order at once.

End.
